newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX crude falls to lowest end in eight months.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX crude falls to lowest end in eight months.

text.p: NYMEX crude ended the month of February with the lowest settlement since late July after selling accelerated in late session when key technical support was breached, traders said.

"We went down a lot at the end with a Wall Street player a heavy seller of April (crude) which pushed it through $20.50. After that, stops were triggered and everyone just nailed it," said a New York crude dealer.
April crude ended 59 cents off at $20.30 a barrel, prompt crude's lowest settlement since July 29, 1996 when it closed at $20.28.
Dealers attributed the breach of $20.50 support to heavy late session selling by brokerage firm J.P. Morgan. Officials at the firm were not immediately available to comment.
Expiry in the refined product March contract Friday sent prompt heat and gasoline lower as traders rolled positions out of March into April.
March gasoline finished down 1.02 cents a gallon at 61.65 cents while March heating oil ended off 1.27 cents at 54.76 cents a gallon.
Dealers said gasoline is showing signs of resilience as its traditional spring rally approaches.

"Products fell because of the expiry. Gasoline may help crude. It (crude) could come back to $21.00. I just don't think it's going to break $20.00," said one trader, adding the April gasoline-to-crude crack spread remained firm, signalling strength in the outright price.
Despite gasolines's sharp losses, the April gasoline crack settled at $5.82 a barrel after closing at $5.87 a barrel Thursday.
Gasoline typically rallies in the spring in anticipation of the summer driving season when demand peaks.

Meanwhile, looming over crude was news Iraqi Foreign Minister Mohammed Saeed al-Sahaf met with the head of the U.N. Humanitarian Affairs Department (DHA) Friday morning, and was said to be asking for increased income from the oil-for-food deal, U.N. officials said.
But, Western diplomats quickly shot down Rasheed's statement, saying no formal request for increased income was seen from Baghdad, and would not be considered at this point.
Under Iraq's agreement with the U.N., sanctions were eased allowing the country to export $2 billion worth of oil every six months, on a renewable basis, in exchange for humanitarian aid.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
